             What You Need to Know About the
             765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 Key facts about the proposed high-voltage lines, the process that produced them, and the questions
                                     that remain unanswered.

1.
Transmission lines don’t generate a single watt of electricity.
They move electricity from somewhere else. Before we commit billions of dollars and thousands of acres,
we should know where that electricity will come from—and whether it will actually be available when
needed.

2.
We’re proposing to import electricity into one of the most energy-rich regions in the
country.
The Permian Basin produces enormous amounts of natural gas. Building generation closer to the
equipment that needs power deserves a serious comparison with sending electricity hundreds of miles
across Texas. “The plan calls for transmission” isn’t that comparison.

3.
The companies building the lines have a financial incentive to build more.
Investor-owned utilities can recover approved investments through rates and earn an authorized return on
the shareholder-funded portion. AEP Texas’s authorized return on equity is 9.76%. That isn’t guaranteed
profit on every dollar spent, but it certainly gives the company a reason to like expensive construction
projects.

4.
You don’t have to live anywhere near a 765 to help pay for it.
Transmission costs are spread among customers across ERCOT. On your electric bill, those costs
generally show up within delivery or transmission-and-distribution charges. The ranch gets the towers.
Customers across the grid get a share of the bill.


5.
These would be the first 765-kV lines in Texas.
Utilities have experience with this voltage elsewhere, but that doesn’t answer every question about building
across Texas ranches, caves, aquifers, quarries, and river crossings. Experience somewhere else still has
to be applied to the actual conditions here.

6.
A 200-foot-wide easement covers about 24 acres for every mile of line.
The landowner usually keeps ownership, but the easement limits what can be done there and gives the
utility ongoing rights. Calling it “just an easement” doesn’t make those restrictions temporary.



                          What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 7.
The Legislature ordered a reliability plan. It did not specifically order 765-kV lines.
House Bill 5066 directed planning for the Permian Basin. The Public Utility Commission—the PUC—made
the decision to use 765s. Those are different decisions made by different people.

8.
The same law cut the transmission approval deadline roughly in half.
In 2023, lawmakers changed the general deadline for deciding new transmission-line applications from one
year to 180 days. These enormous projects then entered a process where landowners had to learn the
rules, examine the evidence, and defend their property on a compressed schedule.


9.
Hundreds of landowners lost their place in the proceedings.
In Howard–Solstice, the PUC’s own final order says MORE THAN HALF of the intervenors were dismissed
for failing to file required testimony or a statement of position. A Dinosaur–Longshore rehearing filing reports
more than 700 dismissals. The Bell County East–Big Hill judges recorded at least 844. These were largely
missed-filing dismissals—not decisions that the underlying property concerns were unfounded.

10.
Much of the projected demand wasn’t backed by signed customer contracts.
In ERCOT’s June 2024 presentation, only 39% of the additional demand outside oil and gas was supported
by contracts. Another 55% relied on letters from utility officers, and 6% was unconfirmed. Those
percentages measure projected electricity demand, not the number of businesses. A letter saying demand
is coming is a different level of commitment from a customer signing a contract.

11.
The original forecast wasn’t simply “all these new AI data centers.”
In that same additional-demand category, 59% was cryptocurrency mining, 22% was green hydrogen, and
6% was data centers. Today’s data-center headlines don’t automatically validate the businesses and
assumptions used in the earlier study.

12.
A proposed business can disappear. An easement is a much longer commitment.
Projects can lose financing, change locations, shrink, or never get built. Before using those proposals to
justify permanent changes to someone else’s property, we need a realistic assessment of which customers
will actually show up.


13.
Changing the assumptions can change how much transmission appears necessary.
Landowners reviewing two ERCOT studies from 2024 identified major differences in the electricity demand
and available generation assumed in each. Different studies can legitimately use different assumptions. But
when those assumptions help justify billions in construction, the differences need to be explained in plain
English.




                           What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 14.
The forecasts have changed while the projects keep moving.
The main Permian transmission study was completed in 2024 and used some earlier inputs. Since then,
proposed customers, generation projects, and forecasting methods have continued changing. Approval
should not become a reason to stop checking whether the original justification still holds.

15.
ERCOT’s comparison found that more than one voltage could meet the reliability
requirements.
Its 2024 comparison showed 345-, 500-, and 765-kV options meeting the reliability criteria studied. The
options had different costs, footprints, losses, and future capabilities. Choosing 765 therefore requires
explaining those tradeoffs—not suggesting every other option failed the reliability test.

16.
The utilities seeking permission didn’t always perform their own alternatives analysis.
The Howard–Solstice final order expressly says the applicants did not independently evaluate alternatives
because the PUC and ERCOT had already evaluated transmission options and directed the applications.
That leaves a fair question about where alternatives such as more local generation received a full
comparison.


17.
These projects were excused from another round of ERCOT review.
Approved Permian-plan projects were exempted from further review through ERCOT’s Regional Planning
Group, where project alternatives would otherwise be considered. Earlier planning did occur, but this
additional review step was removed. With this much money and land involved, that deserves an
explanation.

18.
There is outside analysis challenging the plan.
An economic study commissioned by the Texas Public Policy Foundation argues that additional gas
generation in West Texas, along with changes in where other generation is built, could eliminate the need
for the 765 expansion it examined. That conclusion needs to be tested against ERCOT’s analysis. It
shouldn’t simply disappear from the discussion.

19.
An approved route crosses an active, blasting quarry, with important details left for later.
In Howard–Solstice, landowners raised questions about tower placement, ongoing quarry operations,
engineering feasibility, and cost. The applicants pointed to later engineering and coordination. If solving
those problems could change the route’s cost or practicality, those answers matter before the route is
chosen.




                          What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 20.
“We’ll work that out during engineering” has limits.
Nobody expects every bolt to be designed before approval. But there’s a big difference between finishing a
design and finding out whether a route can safely and reasonably be built. Landowners shouldn’t have to
accept an easement first and hope the important answers work out later.


21.
Texas limestone can have a lot going on underneath it.
Karst terrain can contain caves, fractures, and underground water pathways that aren’t obvious from the
surface. Landowners have requested site-specific drilling and records of how much concrete goes into each
foundation. Those are practical questions about what is underground and how construction will affect it.

22.
A line scheduled for 2030 doesn’t solve next summer’s emergency.
Howard–Solstice’s approved schedule estimates energization in October 2030. Long-term planning matters,
but warnings about immediate shortages should come with immediate solutions. They don’t, by themselves,
establish that this particular long-term project is the right answer.

23.
Major routing changes can arrive right before the vote.
A commissioner’s proposed Howard–Solstice modification was filed the day before the approval meeting.
The memo acknowledged that the change would place 15 additional homes and other occupied buildings
within the relevant distance of the line, along with other impacts. Changes that consequential deserve a
meaningful opportunity for affected people to respond.

24.
Extra protections recommended by the hearing judges can be removed.
In Howard–Solstice, the judges recommended additional measures concerning tribal cultural resources. The
PUC removed those additional requirements and relied on its standard protections. Going through a hearing
and persuading the judges doesn’t necessarily mean those protections survive the final decision.


25.
The campaign money deserves scrutiny.
Reviewed records include two $250,000 contributions to the governor’s campaign from donors with
interests in the routing process for Howard-Solstice. That is half a million dollars. Contributions alone don’t
prove a decision was purchased, but the public deserves transparency about access, conflicts, and how
routing decisions are insulated from political influence.

26.
Public participation should be capable of changing the outcome.
Landowners have asked a basic question: What evidence would cause the PUC to reconsider? If updated
demand, new generation, notice failures, or serious routing problems cannot change the plan, then officials
need to explain what all this public participation is supposed to accomplish.




                           What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 27.
On the northern path, roughly 1,650 additional landowners missed the public-meeting
opportunity.
In Dinosaur–Longshore, administrative judges found that owners affected by links added or modified after
the original meetings had not received public-meeting notice. Later notice of the application did not satisfy
that earlier requirement, according to the judges. The utility disputed that interpretation, and the PUC
ultimately approved the project.

28.
The central path had a similar notice problem affecting roughly 1,400 landowners.
In Bell County East–Big Hill, the judges found that hundreds of miles of possible route links were added
after the public meetings. Newly affected owners missed that early opportunity to identify problems and
suggest changes. The judges considered the failure serious enough to recommend denying the application.


29.
Landowners’ time to join the case was shortened, too.
After the Legislature cut the overall decision deadline, the PUC reduced the normal intervention deadline
from 45 days to 30. The state office representing residential and small-business utility customers opposed
that change, warning about landowners’ ability to defend their property rights. The utilities supported
shortening it.

30.
Some landowners won their way back into a case after the hearing was already over.
In Big Hill–Sand Lake, several people with property interests along the connecting eastern section were
dismissed and later readmitted. The Bell County judges noted that their readmission came too late to
challenge the project’s need at that hearing. The need question was later combined into the Bell County
proceeding, but getting there required another procedural fight.

31.
The central path’s hearing judges said the utilities had not proved it was needed.
Their recommendation covered both Bell County East–Big Hill and Big Hill–Sand Lake. That was a
conclusion from the judges reviewing the evidence, not just an objection from unhappy landowners. The
PUC sent the cases back for additional consideration rather than adopting the recommended denial.

32.
Those judges also asked where the electricity was supposed to come from.
They found the utilities had not established that enough power would be available at Bell County East to
send west through the proposed line. They also identified unanswered questions about serving Central
Texas’s own demand while exporting electricity. That goes straight back to point #1: the line doesn’t make
the power.




                          What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 33.
The judges called part of the demand forecast a “wish list.”
Their criticism concerned the older study used to estimate future oil-and-gas electricity demand. They found
that it relied on desired outcomes and corporate pledges and that changed circumstances undermined its
projections. Before turning those expectations into permanent infrastructure, somebody needs to establish
which expectations still hold up.

34.
A school administrator said a new $4.7 million school building was missing from the maps.
During the Dinosaur–Longshore public argument, she described notifying the utility that its maps did not
show the new building. Her account illustrates why current maps and early local input matter. The people
living and working there may know things that a desktop routing study misses.

35.
Even pipeline companies have challenged the protections.
In Longshore–Drill Hole, pipeline operators sought stronger requirements addressing electrical interference
with their pipelines, including crossings and coordination before the line is energized. The utility opposed
those additions, arguing that the PUC’s standard requirements were sufficient. Questions about these lines
aren’t coming only from landowners who dislike the view.

36.
New generation in West Texas deserves the same attention as new demand.
In the Bell County proceeding, landowners presented evidence of dozens of announced or planned
gas-generation projects, and the judges found that evidence warranted considering whether the lines could
be reduced or avoided. Announcements aren’t operating power plants—but that same caution should apply
when counting proposed electricity customers.


37.
The Legislature itself said existing protections weren’t enough.
In SB 75, passed in 2025, lawmakers expressly found that existing incentives and regulations were
insufficient to make utilities prioritize grid security and resilience. They created the Texas Grid Security
Commission to evaluate threats and recommend improvements. For the 765s, that means the discussion
should include storm damage, sabotage, equipment failures, backup options, and recovery times. Moving
more electricity is useful. Being able to keep operating—or recover quickly—when something goes wrong
matters, too.

38.
Cybersecurity includes who can get into the equipment.
SB 2116, the 2021 Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act, restricts agreements giving certain companies
direct or remote access to Texas’s critical infrastructure. Its restrictions depend on ownership, control, or
headquarters connections to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and other designated countries. For a major
grid expansion, scrutiny should extend to equipment suppliers, software, maintenance arrangements, and
remote access. We need to know who verifies compliance and how—not simply that a law exists.




                          What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 39.
The connections between the energy industry, state leadership, and regulators deserve
scrutiny.
Oncor’s own website lists the governor’s former chief of staff as a board member. The governor appoints
the PUC commissioners who regulate the company. Meanwhile, the PUC chairman’s wife serves as deputy
director of the governor’s Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office, where she leads the design and
administration of a $350 million nuclear-development grant program. Those relationships don’t prove that a
765-kV decision was improper. They do deserve disclosure and clear safeguards against conflicts of
interest. Texans should be able to understand how decisions affecting our property, electric bills, and public
money are kept independent.

40.
SB 6 doesn’t automatically put the entire bill on the companies driving the growth.
Texas’s 2025 Senate Bill 6 requires financial commitments and contributions toward connection costs from
covered large electricity customers. It also directs the PUC to review how transmission costs are divided
among customers. But paying to connect a facility and paying for the broader grid expansion are different
things. Before anyone tells us “the data centers will pay,” show us which costs they must cover, which costs
reach everybody else’s bill, and who pays if a proposed customer never shows up.


41.
Texas put deadlines on its new grid-security work.
SB 75 requires the Texas Grid Security Commission to deliver recommended resilience standards and a
plan for protecting critical infrastructure by December 1, 2026. It also requires the PUC and ERCOT to
conduct a physical-attack preparedness exercise with electricity providers by December 31, 2026. Those
requirements don’t automatically stop transmission approvals. But their findings should inform the 765
buildout while there is still time to change designs, equipment, or safeguards. Security recommendations
are more useful before billions are committed than after everything is built.

42.
The foreign-access law includes an exception for warranty and support.
The Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act allows specifically authorized access for product warranty and
support purposes. That matters when equipment depends on software updates, troubleshooting, or remote
maintenance. In April 2026, ERCOT itself suggested that lawmakers consider requiring security measures
for this authorized access. We should be asking what access is allowed, who approves it, how it is
monitored, and how it can be shut off. An exception written into a law still needs practical safeguards.

43.
ERCOT’s own records show widespread delays in required security reporting.
In an April 2026 presentation, ERCOT reported that only 625 of 1,704 required market participants
submitted their critical-grid-equipment and services reports on time. Another 953 filed late, and 126 were
nonresponsive. By that presentation, most of the nonresponsive participants had left the market or been
terminated; ERCOT and the PUC were addressing the remaining nine. Those are grid-wide figures, not a
finding against a particular 765 applicant. They don’t prove prohibited access occurred. They do show why
“companies are required to report” is not enough assurance by itself.




                          What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas
 44.
Regulators have tools to check these claims—and penalties for covered violations.
Later legislation strengthened the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act’s enforcement. SB 2368, passed
in 2025, allows ERCOT to demand additional information to verify required reports and certifications. It also
authorizes PUC penalties of up to $1 million per violation for specified violations, including failing to provide
required information or knowingly providing false information. Oversight can go beyond collecting a signed
form. Texans deserve to know what verification and enforcement stand behind the assurances we’re being
given.



    These points are drawn from public records, PUC orders, hearing recommendations, ERCOT
                                presentations, and related filings.




                           What You Need to Know About the 765-kV Transmission Lines in Texas

SB 75 requires the Texas Grid Security Commission to deliver recommended resilience standards and a
plan for protecting critical infrastructure by December 1, 2026. It also requires the PUC and ERCOT to
conduct a physical-attack preparedness exercise with electricity providers by December 31, 2026. Those
requirements don't automatically stop transmission approvals. But their findings should inform the 765
buildout while there is still time to change designs, equipment, or safeguards. Security recommendations
are more useful before billions are committed than after everything is built.

42.
The foreign-access law includes an exception for warranty and support.
The Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act allows specifically authorized access for product warranty and
support purposes. That matters when equipment depends on software updates, troubleshooting, or remote
maintenance. In April 2026, ERCOT itself suggested that lawmakers consider requiring security measures
for this authorized access. We should be asking what access is allowed, who approves it, how it is
monitored, and how it can be shut off. An exception written into a law still needs practical safeguards.

43.
ERCOT's own records show widespread delays in required security reporting.
In an April 2026 presentation, ERCOT reported that only 625 of 1,704 required market participants
submitted their critical-grid-equipment and services reports on time. Another 953 filed late, and 126 were
nonresponsive. By that presentation, most of the nonresponsive participants had left the market or been
terminated; ERCOT and the PUC were addressing the remaining nine. Those are grid-wide figures, not a
finding against a particular 765 applicant. They don't prove prohibited access occurred. They do show why
"companies are required to report" is not enough assurance by itself.

 44.
Regulators have tools to check these claims-and penalties for covered violations.
Later legislation strengthened the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act's enforcement. SB 2368, passed
in 2025, allows ERCOT to demand additional information to verify required reports and certifications. It also
authorizes PUC penalties of up to $1 million per violation for specified violations, including failing to provide
required information or knowingly providing false information. Oversight can go beyond collecting a signed
form. Texans deserve to know what verification and enforcement stand behind the assurances we're being
given.
